newsitem.title: usa: New fund first to aim at gay men, women.
newsitem.headline: New fund first to aim at gay men, women.

text.p: In what appears to be the first of its kind, a new mutual fund has been launched that is being marketed directly at homosexual men and women.
The fund buys only securities of companies with policies that it views as "gay friendly."
"We won't invest in companies unless they have a progressive policy towards gays and lesbians," said Shelly Meyers, portfolio manager of the Meyers, Sheppard Pride Fund.
The 37-year-old Meyers, an MBA who describes herself as gay, said that her work in the investment industry convinced her there was a need in the market for such a fund.

Started in June, the Meyers, Sheppard Pride Fund looks for companies with personnel policies that explicitly prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation, and those that offer health benefits to homosexual partners.
Two fund-tracking firms said the fund appears to be the first to have such criteria.

Meyers said the fund has identified about 400 companies that meet its guidelines, including about 200 of those in the Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks. That compares with a total of about 6,000 corporations with publicly traded stock in the United States.

Meyers said she has found that the technology, financial services and consumer services sectors have a higher proportion of companies that are "gay friendly," with utilities and energy among the least friendly.
The fund's investment philosophy is value-oriented, seeking equities that are undervalued, she said.

The fund uses so-called momentum investing -- seeking out companies with rising earnings, a change in product mix or a significant management overhaul -- as well as traditional criteria such as stock price compared with a company's underlying value.

The fund has about 40 issues in its portfolio, and ranges between 35 and 55 stocks. Its top five holdings are: Arrow Electronics Inc., McKesson Corp., Time Warner Inc., Glendale Federal Bank and American Express Co.
Through last Friday, the fund has returned 4.1 percent, Meyers said. According to Morningstar Inc., which tracks fund performance, the average fund in the category returned 4.56 percent.
Meyers said the fund has about $800,000 in total assets. New funds often find it hard to reach $1 million at first, but she said she expected to cross that barrier soon.
She expected assets to grow to about $35 million by next June. The fund is aimed at individual and institutional investors.

Meyers said the firm has made distribution deals with Furman Selz, an investment bank that also markets mutual funds, and Jack White & Co., a discount brokerage, and is negotiating with Charles Schwab, another discount broker.
Born and raised in Wixom, Mich., Meyers got her undergraduate degree from the University of Michigan and a Masters in Business Administration from Dartmouth College's Amos Tuck School of Business.
She started with the Boston Co., first as an industry analyst and later as a portfolio manager in its institutional asset management group in Los Angeles.
